novelty.justification: The idea explicitly centers on a 'mutant-set-preserving observability harness' and 'causal 2×2 factorial measurement protocol' rather than inventing wholly new observability techniques. This meaningfully extends prior work such as bytecode analysis for observability (R19), automated testability refactoring (R52), and observability/mutation correlation studies (R58), but the solution approach remains within known bytecode-instrumentation/testability-transformation territory.
novelty.rubric: Incremental: a meaningful extension or optimization of prior baseline work that fixes a concrete prior limitation, but the core paradigm is unchanged.
novelty.differentiation: The core idea of improving observability via bytecode/refactoring transformations already appears in R19, R52, and R54, while R58 and R11 study observability/testability and mutation effectiveness. The proposed differentiator is a mutant-set-preserving ASM harness with recursive observability and a causal 2x2 factorial protocol to isolate state visibility versus composed-object visibility.

feasibility.justification: The plan requires nontrivial engineering: building an ASM-based transform with recursive type-closure getters, running a 2x2 factorial across multiple seeds, and validating mutation-set preservation. However, it uses pre-mounted SF110/EvoSuite and states 'Verified end-to-end under Java 11', so this is a moderate but realistic research-engineering effort.
feasibility.rubric: Moderate workload (sweet spot): needs nontrivial coding such as scripting existing open-source tools (parsers, CFG extractors) or building a custom graph-processing pipeline; standard research engineering effort.

clarity.justification: The proposal is concrete: it specifies a '2×2 factorial' design, ASM-appended getters that contain 'no arithmetic/logic instructions' to avoid new mutants, recursive observability with depth ≤ 3, and 'Vargha-Delaney A12 + one-tailed Wilcoxon pooled across seeds'. Some details, such as exact class-filtering criteria and seed counts, are underspecified but the overall plan is clear.
clarity.rubric: Clear and concrete: steps are explicit with a reasonable, specific experiment design (baseline tools, metric definitions); can be turned into a solid proposal.

idea_generation.summary: The idea proposes a bytecode-level observability restoration harness to measure how exposing private/protected fields and composed-object internals affects EvoSuite mutation scores. It is a feasible incremental extension of prior testability/observability work, with a strong experimental design using a 2x2 factorial and statistical effect-size analysis. The main novelty is the mutant-set-preserving instrumentation and causal isolation of two observability deficits, though the underlying technique is not paradigm-changing.
strengths: Clear causal 2x2 factorial design isolating hidden state vs composed-object observability
Mutant-set-preserving ASM instrumentation is a thoughtful confound control
Concrete metrics and statistical tests are specified
Builds on available offline tools and reports an end-to-end smoke test
weaknesses: Core observability-restoration technique is already present in the solution space
Exact class selection and seed sweep details are not fully specified
Recursive type-closure getter injection may still introduce subtle assertion or coverage changes

original.overall_conclusion: Improving class observability in EvoSuite by injecting public accessors for private/protected attributes and enabling recursive assertions on complex object state significantly improves generated tests' mutation scores for a subset of classes. The injected getters provide the main benefit, while recursive assertions add only limited further improvement.
original.comparable_notes: Evaluation used 100 SF110 Java classes filtered by cyclomatic complexity threshold of 3, with EvoSuite/DynaMOSA as baseline. Test generation used 30 seeds per class, producing 12,000 test suites total. Comparison used one-tailed Wilcoxon tests at alpha=0.05 and Vargha-Delaney A12 effect sizes. Injected accessors and recursive assertions were excluded from test goals and mutation score computation. Mutation score was measured over 26,177 total generated mutants.

results_paper_consistency.method: Direct LLM comparison: agent's FINAL results artifact (metrics.json summary) vs paper Results/Discussion/Conclusion. Interim failed runs are NOT evidence unless still present in the final metrics file.
results_paper_consistency.justification: The available paper excerpt contains only front/back matter and section commands; no detailed results or discussion text is visible beyond the title. The title claims that hidden state and opaque composed objects depress mutation-based effectiveness. Final results partially support this: the composed-object effect is significant but tiny (RQ2 mutation A12=.505, p=.0022), while the hidden-state effect is not statistically significant (RQ1 mutation A12=.497, p=.0704). Thus the title's hidden-state claim is overstated, but there is no evidence of deliberate concealment of final negative outcomes.
supported_claims: Composed objects are associated with a statistically significant but very small mutation-score decrease (RQ2 A12=.505, p=.0022).
Combined configuration achieves small significant mutation-score improvements over baseline and getters (A12=.512/.515, p<.004).
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Title implication that hidden state depresses mutation-based effectiveness is not statistically supported by the final RQ1 hidden-state result (p=.0704, A12=.497).
unfavorable_in_final_results: RQ1 hidden-state mutation difference is non-significant and negligible.
RQ2 composed-object mutation decrease is significant but very small (about 0.0007 mean difference).
results_paper_consistency.rubric: Mixed: overall story roughly matches, but some claims are overstated or some negative cells are under-discussed.
